power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background Systemic sclerosis (SSc) and dermatomyositis (DM) are autoimmune diseases that have been proposed as models of cancer immunoediting.
Autoantibody-defined subsets show divergent cancer risks, yet malignancy often remains clinically occult.
We tested whether circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) can reveal subclinical cancer in new-onset SSc and DM.
We prospectively recruited adults with recent SSc or DM onset.
Plasma ctDNA was assessed using a targeted next-generation sequencing panel covering commonly mutated cancer genes.
Patients were followed for 18-24 months on average. ctDNA positivity was correlated with subsequent cancer diagnoses.

Findings Among 134 patients (69 SSc, 65 DM), cancer was diagnosed in six (4•5%; three SSc, three DM). ctDNA was detected in four of these six patients (67%) a median of 13 months (range 1•4-17) before clinical diagnosis; in three of four patients, mutations detected in plasma matched those subsequently identified in the same patients' primary tumors. ctDNA was also detected in 16 of 128 patients without a cancer diagnosis. ctDNA positivity conferred an 11•4fold higher risk of malignancy relative to ctDNA negativity and yielded a negative predictive value of 98% and a positive predictive value of 20% for cancer within the observation window.
Interpretation ctDNA testing identified most cancers that emerged within 18 months in newonset SSc and DM and stratified near-term cancer risk.

These findings support larger, interventional trials to determine whether ctDNA-guided surveillance improves timeliness of cancer detection, optimizes imaging and biopsy strategies, and enhances outcomes in patients with SSc and DM.

Evidence before this study: Patients with new onset systemic sclerosis (SSc) and dermatomyositis (DM) have an increased risk of contemporaneous cancer in distinct autoantibody subgroups, and mechanistic studies suggest that these patients may have cancerinduced autoimmunity.
The optimal approach to cancer detection, and whether subclinical malignancy may be present in patients with new onset rheumatic disease, remains unknown.
We show that circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is present in ~15% of patients with new onset SSc and DM.
Patients with ctDNA have a higher risk of subsequent malignancy, with data suggesting that it can detect cancer earlier than conventional methods in this patient population.
These findings suggest that subclinical malignancy may be present in a subset of patients with new onset SSc and DM and that ctDNA may be a valuable tool to risk stratify patients for cancer.
The relationship between cancer and autoimmunity has attracted increasing attention over the past two decades.
The concept of cancer immunoediting, encompassing the processes of cancer elimination, equilibrium, and escape, has been central to elucidating interactions between the immune system and cancer.
This framework has advanced understanding of both effective immune surveillance and immune dysregulation, including the emergence of autoimmune phenomena.

Systemic sclerosis (SSc) and dermatomyositis (DM) are two autoimmune rheumatic diseases characterized by a substantial association with cancer in patient subgroups defined by distinct autoantibodies (1, 2).

text.text: For example, patients with anti-RNA polymerase III (POLR3)positive SSc and anti-TIF1γ-positive DM have an increased risk of cancer within 3 years of rheumatic disease onset.

Prior research has identified genetic alterations, including somatic mutations and loss of heterozygosity in the POLR3A and TRIM33 genes which encode POLR3 and TIF1γ, respectively, in tumors from patients with anti-POLR3-positive SSc and anti-TIF1γpositive DM (3) (4).

text.text: Furthermore, in patients with SSc, it has been shown that there are mutationspecific T cell and cross-reactive autoantibody responses to both mutated and wildtype forms of these antigens.

Collectively, these findings suggest that an immune response initiated by somatic mutations in emerging tumors may inadvertently result in the targeting of healthy tissues, thereby triggering autoimmunity (5).

text.text: Over the last decade, this emerging model has been supported by additional studies (6) (7) (8), reinforcing the concept that the immune system's responses to tumors can have far-reaching consequences, in some cases leading to autoimmune disease.

text.text: Multiple studies have shown that only a subset of anti-POLR3-positive SSc and anti-TIF1γpositive DM patients develop clinically detectable cancer (1-2, 6-8).
One explanation for this heterogeneity is that the immune responses to POLR3 and TIF1γ might be induced by multiple mechanisms, with cancer being only one of these.
Alternately, it is possible that cancer is a driver of these autoimmune responses in all patients within these serologically-defined subsets.

The second explanation posits that in some patients, the immune system may successfully hold a nascent tumor in equilibrium preventing its progression to a clinically manifest cancer, perhaps even destroying the cancer.
Support for this idea comes from studies showing that patients with specific SSc and DM autoantibodies have a lower than expected risk of cancer (1, 2).
In particular, patients with SSc and anti-POLR3 plus anti-RNA polymerase 1 (POLR1) or anticentromere (CENP) antibodies have a lower cancer risk relative to the general population.
Additionally, breast cancer patients without SSc who have anti-CENP antibodies have improved cancer survival (9).

text.text: In other patients, the immune response is not strong enough to control tumor progression, and clinically manifest cancer.
Note that in both of these hypothetical scenarios, the cancer precedes the autoimmune disease.

Until recently, technological limitations restricted the detection and monitoring of early malignancies to modalities such as whole body [ 18 F] fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (FDG-PET/CT) imaging and flow cytometry).
The advent of liquid biopsy technologies, which enable detection of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) (10) (11) (12), has broadened this potential.

text.text: In the current study, we aimed to determine whether ctDNA could be detected in patients with early onset SSc and DM prior to clinical presentation of cancer.
We conducted a prospective observational cohort study across two disease-specific centers, recruiting 134 patients from the Johns Hopkins Division of Rheumatology Scleroderma and Myositis Centers.
Eligible patients had either SSc meeting 2013 ACR/EULAR criteria or DM meeting 2017 ACR/EULAR criteria, age ≥ 18 years, and a disease duration of less than 3 years.
No history of cancer within 3 years of disease onset was allowed, excluding non-melanoma skin cancer.
Patient recruitment began in November 2018, initially targeting individuals with SSc who were anti-POLR3 positive.
In 2021, the criteria were expanded to include all patients with SSc, regardless of autoantibody status, to enable comparisons across serologic subgroups.
Eligible DM patients were recruited consecutively for enrollment starting in May of 2022.
The study protocols were approved by the Johns Hopkins Institutional Review Board (NA_00036834 and IRB00235256).
Written informed consent was obtained from participants prior to study participation.
All patients were followed longitudinally at the Johns Hopkins Scleroderma and Myositis Centers.
All 134 patients had at least one blood sample collected.
Of these, 73 had a second sample collected at least 3 months after the first.

text.text: The outcomes of interest were ctDNA positivity and a clinical cancer diagnosis.

Only patients who had biopsy proven histopathologic diagnosis of invasion were classified as having cancer; patients with benign tumors, including non-invasive in situ tumors of the skin, were not classified as having cancer.
Statistical tests were performed to assess whether there were differences in demographic, clinical and autoantibody characteristics between ctDNA-positive and ctDNA-negative patients.
Detailed definitions and autoantibody assay methods are provided in the Supplement.
The Student's t-test was used for continuous variables and Fisher's exact test for categorical variables.
The Benjamini-Hochberg method was used to correct for multiple comparisons.
All analyses were performed using R version 4•3•2.

text.text: Thus, ctDNA positivity was associated with a 11•4-fold higher risk of subclinical malignancy compared with ctDNA negativity, with a negative predictive value of 98% and a positive predictive value of 20%.
Compelling epidemiologic and mechanistic studies suggest that cancer may drive the development of autoimmunity in subgroups of patients with SSc and DM identified by distinct autoantibody responses.
However, most patients within these autoantibody subgroups do not have a clinically diagnosed cancer.

In this study, we detected evidence of cancer, through analysis of ctDNA in blood, in four of six patients who developed a clinically detectable cancer at a median of 13 months prior to clinical diagnosis.
Of note, in two of these 4 cancers, diagnostic PET/CTs around the time of ctDNA positivity were unremarkable, highlighting the potential value of ctDNA assessment as a cancer screening tool.

One striking finding of our work is that of 20 patients with detectable ctDNA mutations, only four developed a clinically detectable cancer despite intensive cancer surveillance over the ensuing months.
And in one (SCL 200) of the four patients with a positive ctDNA test, the mutation was not identified in the patient's subsequent cancer biopsy tissue.

Though the nominal positive predictive value (PPV 20%) of our test was higher than that for mammography for breast cancer or spiral CT for lung cancer, it is still lower than optimal from an interventional standpoint.
There are at least two hypotheses to explain the low PPV.

The most intellectually exciting of these is that more of these ctDNA-positive patients actually had cancer, but the cancer was not large enough to cause symptoms or to be detected by routine surveillance measures.
According to this hypothesis, some of the ctDNA-positive patients will be diagnosed with cancer in the future.
Indeed, ctDNA can be detected up to three years prior to clinical cancer diagnosis (13), and the median follow-up time for patients in the current study was only 17 months.
The presence of cell-free DNA but the absence of clinically detectable cancer could accordingly represent a state of equilibrium between the immune system and cancer (7).
text.formatted: The presence of cell-free DNA but the absence of clinically detectable cancer could accordingly represent a state of equilibrium between the immune system and cancer <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: This hypothesis is consistent with the underlying rationale for our study, i.e., the immune response elicited by the tumor is sufficient to inhibit its progression, sometimes to the extent that clinical cancer never appears.
The other hypotheses explain the ctDNA-positives as either technical or biological artifacts, so there is no cancer at all present in the patients with positive ctDNA results.
When the same ctDNA test is applied to young healthy individuals, false positives are rare, so technical artifacts are minimized (15).
text.formatted: When the same ctDNA test is applied to young healthy individuals, false positives are rare, so technical artifacts are minimized <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref>.

text.text: However, biological "artifacts" are still possible.
The most likely type of biological artifact is clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP).

Though we evaluated very large numbers of molecules to confidently exclude leukocyte DNA mutations in even a minor fraction of leukocytes, we could not exclude mutations that arose from an even smaller fraction of lymphocytes, such as those that contributed cfDNA in excess of their representation in peripheral blood counts.
Prior studies using DNA methylation have indeed shown that B-lymphocytes contribute more cfDNA than expected from their peripheral blood cell fraction (20).

text.text: Longitudinal monitoring of circulating tumor DNA mutations, paired with clinical phenotyping of patients' disease activity and autoantibody profiles, is currently underway to test these relationships.
A noteworthy strength of our study design was to purposefully focus on patients with newly diagnosed autoimmune disease (<3 years), as this is the population at highest risk of cancer diagnosis.

text.text: Additionally, our inclusion of patients with a broad range of autoantibodies with different epidemiologic cancer associations was informative.

Multiple epidemiologic studies have shown that specific autoantibody profiles stratify cancer risk within the first three years after rheumatic disease onset, with some profiles associated with increased risk, others with decreased risk, and others with no change (1, 2).

text.text: However, several of the ctDNA positive patients had autoantibodies, such as anti-centromere, that have been linked to a decreased cancer risk in cohort studies or when compared to the general population.

A potential explanation is that these autoantibody specificities are a surrogate for a highly effective anti-tumor immune response, accounting for the negative association observed in prior epidemiologic studies.
It is noteworthy that among the six SSc patients who had an initial positive ctDNA test followed by a negative test, three had anti-centromere antibodies (SCL250, SCL252, SCL254).
Our study has several limitations.
While we tried to employ systematic cancer screening strategies, not all patients underwent recommended tests in part due to the Covid-19 pandemic, and in part due to patient preference.

Only a subset of patients had a second sample available for ctDNA analysis, and an important priority is examining the dynamic relationship between ctDNA levels, evolution of the immune response, and cancer emergence over time.
As noted above, the follow-up time is relatively short, so the false-positive rate may be overestimated.
And the relatively small number (n=six) of patients that developed cancer in this cohort engender wide confidence limits in all of the reported outcomes.
What are the potential clinical implications of our findings?
From a rheumatology perspective, the earlier detection and treatment of cancer may lead to improvement, if not remission, of the rheumatic disease [23] [24].

text.text: From an oncologic perspective, the earlier detection of cancer could lead to improved survival, and even cure, of the cancers.
There is evidence that a delay of even a month between diagnosis of a cancer and its surgical removal has a substantial effect on survival (25) (26) (27).
text.formatted: There is evidence that a delay of even a month between diagnosis of a cancer and its surgical removal has a substantial effect on survival <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(26)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(27)</ref>.

text.text: And there is also much data indicating that anti-cancer drugs of all types are much more likely to induce prolonged remissions or cures when a smaller tumor burden is present at the time of treatment (28) (29) (30).
text.formatted: And there is also much data indicating that anti-cancer drugs of all types are much more likely to induce prolonged remissions or cures when a smaller tumor burden is present at the time of treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(30)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, the relatively high ctDNA positive rate observed in our study is concerning, as it could lead to additional anxiety, or needless procedures, in patients who already have a serious autoimmune disease.

In summary, we have unequivocally shown that the cancers in some patients with specific types of autoimmune diseases can be detected with a blood test before conventional methods are able to detect them.
This study thereby sets the stage for larger, prospective studies to determine whether such testing can benefit patients.
